title: Cell structure and levels of organisation

beats.say: Open like a teacher: every living thing is built from cells, and a cell is a tiny factory with parts. No questions.

lines.text: cells are the basic units of all living things
lines.say: Every living thing is made of cells. They're so small that we measure them in micrometres, which are thousandths of a millimetre. Inside, a cell is like a tiny factory, with different parts doing different jobs.

beats.say: The animal cell parts and jobs: membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes. Explain each with a colour. No questions.

lines.text: {{cell membrane|ul.b}}  -  a barrier that controls what goes in and out
lines.say: First the outside. The cell membrane is a thin barrier that is partially permeable: it lets some things through, and stops others.

lines.text: {{cytoplasm|ul.g}}  -  where chemical reactions happen
lines.say: Inside is the cytoplasm, a jelly-like liquid where many of the cell's chemical reactions happen.

lines.text: {{nucleus|ul.p}}  -  holds DNA, controls the cell
lines.say: The nucleus holds the DNA, the instructions that control what the cell does.

lines.text: {{mitochondria|ul}}  -  release energy by aerobic respiration
lines.say: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens, releasing energy.

lines.text: {{ribosomes|ul.b}}  -  make proteins
lines.say: And ribosomes are where the cell builds proteins.

beats.say: Plant cell extras: cellulose cell wall, large permanent vacuole with cell sap, chloroplasts with chlorophyll. Plant cells also have everything an animal cell has. No questions.

lines.text: plant cell  =  everything in an animal cell, PLUS three extras
lines.say: A plant cell has everything an animal cell has, and three extra things.

lines.text: {{cell wall|ul.p}}  -  tough, made of cellulose, supports and shapes the cell
lines.say: One, a cell wall made of cellulose. It's tough and gives the cell its shape and support.

lines.text: {{large vacuole|ul.b}}  -  holds cell sap
lines.say: Two, a large permanent vacuole filled with a liquid called cell sap.

lines.text: {{chloroplasts|ul.g}}  -  contain chlorophyll, make food by photosynthesis
lines.say: Three, chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis. But only in green parts of the plant.

beats.say: A friend says plant cells have a cell wall instead of a membrane, and that all plant cells have chloroplasts. Test both. Detective tone, no questions.

board.text: A friend's ideas about plant cells

lines.text: cell wall only?
lines.say: A friend of mine says plant cells have a cell wall, so they don't need a membrane. Let's test that.

lines.text: The cell wall lets almost everything through
lines.say: A cellulose wall is fully permeable. It holds the shape but it lets water and dissolved substances pass freely.

lines.text: The membrane inside the wall CONTROLS what enters and leaves
lines.say: So there is still a membrane just inside the wall, and it's the membrane that controls what goes in and out. Plant cells have both.

lines.text: root cell underground:  no light  →  no chloroplasts
lines.say: Second claim: all plant cells have chloroplasts. A root cell is underground, in the dark. Chloroplasts would be useless there, so root cells don't have them.

lines.text: Only green, light-exposed cells have chloroplasts
lines.say: Only the green cells that are exposed to light, such as in leaves, have chloroplasts.

beats.say: A friend says the nucleus is the brain of the cell. Test: a cell has no thoughts; the nucleus stores DNA instructions. Detective tone, no questions.

board.text: A friend's idea: the nucleus is the brain

lines.text: Is the nucleus a brain?
lines.say: A friend of mine calls the nucleus the cell's brain, that it thinks and decides. Let's test that.

lines.text: A cell has no nerves and no thoughts
lines.say: A single cell has no nerves and cannot think.

lines.text: The nucleus stores DNA: a set of instructions, like a recipe book
lines.say: What the nucleus actually does is store the DNA, a coded set of instructions, like a recipe book. Other parts, such as ribosomes, read the instructions and build proteins.

beats.say: Specialised cells: red blood cell (biconcave, no nucleus, haemoglobin), root hair cell (long projection), ciliated cell (cilia sweep mucus). Shape fits function. No questions.

lines.text: Red blood cell:  biconcave disc, no nucleus, full of haemoglobin
lines.say: A red blood cell is shaped like a disc with a dip on each side, has no nucleus, and is packed with haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

lines.text: Root hair cell:  a long thin projection
lines.say: A root hair cell has a long, thin projection that gives it a large surface to take in water and minerals from the soil.

lines.text: Ciliated cell:  tiny hairs (cilia) that sweep mucus
lines.say: A ciliated cell has tiny hairs called cilia that sweep mucus along.

lines.text: Shape fits job
lines.say: In each case, the shape of the cell fits its job. That is what specialised means.

beats.say: Levels of organisation: organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. Use the heart muscle for a worked example. No questions.

lines.text: organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
lines.say: Cells aren't the end of the story. Living things are built up in levels, starting with the tiny parts inside a cell and finishing with the whole living thing.

lines.text: A mitochondrion is an organelle inside a heart muscle cell
lines.say: Take the heart. A mitochondrion is an organelle, a small part, inside a heart muscle cell.

lines.text: Many muscle cells together  =  muscle tissue
lines.say: A group of similar cells doing the same job is a tissue, like heart muscle tissue.

lines.text: Different tissues together  =  an organ  (the heart)
lines.say: Different tissues working together make an organ, the heart.

lines.text: Organs together  =  an organ system  (circulatory system)
lines.say: Organs working together make an organ system, like the circulatory system. And all the systems together make the whole organism.

beats.say: Do it TOGETHER: structure jobs. Questions written on the board first.

lines.text: mitochondria     ribosomes     cell wall     chloroplasts
lines.say: Now you help me match some structures to their jobs.

lines.text: Mitochondria: release energy (aerobic respiration)
lines.say: Yes.

ask.prompt: What is the job of mitochondria?
ask.lookFor: They release energy by aerobic respiration.
ask.onMiss: Ask: which life process releases energy?

lines.text: Ribosomes: make proteins
lines.say: Right.

ask.onMiss: Ask: they follow the DNA's instructions to build what?

lines.text: Only in plant cells: cell wall, large vacuole, chloroplasts
lines.say: Last.

ask.prompt: Name one structure found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
ask.lookFor: Any of: cellulose cell wall, large permanent vacuole, chloroplasts.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what gives a plant cell its stiff shape? What makes its food?

beats.say: The child works alone: order these levels: tissue, organism, cell, organ; and why a root hair cell has a long projection. Hints only if stuck.

lines.text: tissue     organism     cell     organ
lines.say: Your turn to lead. Four levels in a jumble.

lines.text: cell → tissue → organ → organism
lines.say: Put them in order.

ask.prompt: Put these in order, smallest to largest.
ask.onMiss: Ask: which one is made of cells that are alike? Which is made of different tissues?

lines.text: Long projection  →  large surface area to take in water and minerals
lines.say: And one about adaptation.

ask.prompt: Why does a root hair cell have a long, thin projection?
ask.lookFor: It gives a large surface area for taking in water and minerals from the soil.
ask.onMiss: Ask: does a bigger surface take in more or less?

beats.say: Why a membrane is needed even with a wall. Reward reasoning.

board.text: Say it in your own words

lines.text: wall AND membrane
lines.say: Last one.

ask.prompt: Why does a plant cell need a cell membrane when it already has a cell wall?
ask.lookFor: The wall is fully permeable and only supports the cell; the membrane controls what enters and leaves.
ask.onMiss: Ask: does the wall stop substances getting through, or the membrane?
